concept.name: Hanging man
concept.definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the top of the range, a long lower shadow (conventionally two or more times the body), and little or no upper shadow, appearing after an uptrend. It has the same shape as a hammer; technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal warning because the deep intraperiod selloff revealed latent selling pressure, though the reading requires bearish confirmation.
concept.intuition: Price was dumped hard during the session and only partly recovered; the fact that sellers could push it that low at all, after a long rise, is taken as a crack in the uptrend.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: identical geometry to the hammer (small body near the high, lower shadow >= ~2x body, minimal upper shadow); the distinguishing feature is context, since it must follow an advance. Confirmation is typically a lower close on the following candle.
concept.failure_modes: The recovery to near the open shows buyers are still active, so many hanging men are followed by further gains; acting short without confirmation has a high failure rate. In strong trends it repeatedly fails as a topping signal.
concept.misconceptions: The shape alone does not make a hanging man: the same candle after a decline is a hammer, a bullish sign. Nor is a hanging man an immediate sell signal; it is a warning that needs a confirming down candle.
concept.example: After a steady six-week climb, a stock opens at 70.00, plunges to 66.00 intraday, and closes at 69.80. Chartists flag the hanging man and wait; a close below 68.50 the next day would confirm the bearish reading.
